Widow rockfish (Sebastes entomelas) attain a maximum total length of 60 centimeters [Li = 60 centimeters], placing them among the larger members of the genus Sebastes along the northeastern Pacific continental shelf. Field surveys conducted by the Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife using bottom trawls have recorded individuals approaching this asymptotic size in the deep reef habitats off the coast of northern California. The length-weight relationship derived from these same surveys indicates that a fish at this maximum size corresponds to an ultimate wet weight of approximately 2,800 grams [Wwi = approximately 2,800 grams], a value consistent with the robust, deep-bodied morphology characteristic of this species. This substantial body mass is achieved through a prolonged growth trajectory that spans several decades, reflecting the slow-to-moderate growth rates typical of many rockfishes. Younger, pre-reproductive individuals exhibit considerably lower body masses, with the transition to sexual maturity accompanied by a significant increase in both length and somatic investment.

Puberty in Sebastes entomelas is reached at a total length of 36 centimeters [Lp = 36 centimeters], a size threshold that corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of 644 grams [Wwp = 644 grams]. This reproductive milestone typically occurs between four and six years of age depending on local oceanographic conditions, with females maturing slightly later than males on average. Histological examination of ovarian tissue from specimens collected during NOAA's groundfish surveys reveals that vitellogenesis is initiated once this size-based threshold is surpassed. The transition from juvenile to mature reproductive status represents a critical life-history shift, as metabolic resources must now support both continued somatic growth and the demands of gamete production. Individuals below this length are rarely observed in gravid condition, confirming the functional importance of this size-based puberty threshold in regulating the onset of reproductive activity within the population.

Reproductive output in Widow rockfish is strongly influenced by ambient water temperature, with experimental laboratory studies conducted at a stable temperature of 5.6 °C [T = 5.6 °C] providing the most reliable estimates of fecundity. Under these thermal conditions, which mirror the typical bottom temperatures of their adult habitat, females are estimated to extrude approximately 3,000 larvae per day [Ri = approximately 3,000 larvae per day] during the peak of the spawning season. This high daily larval production is sustained over a spawning period that lasts several weeks, yielding an annual fecundity on the order of tens of thousands of offspring. The dependence of reproductive rate on temperature is biologically significant; deviations from this optimal thermal regime have been linked to reduced larval viability and lower overall recruitment success in field populations. The larval output at this temperature is among the highest recorded for any Sebastes species of comparable body size.

The mass of individual larvae at parturition is exceptionally small, reflecting the extreme fecundity of this viviparous species. Neonate wet weight at birth has been estimated at 0.000268 grams [Wwb = 0.000268 grams], based on the mean egg diameter of approximately 0.8 millimeters observed in gravid females examined during late gestation. This miniature body size is a direct consequence of the maternal strategy of producing vast numbers of small offspring, a trade-off that maximizes the probability of population persistence in a variable pelagic environment. Newly extruded larvae are lecithotrophic, relying on endogenous yolk reserves for the first several days of exogenous feeding. The yolk-sac stage is brief, lasting only a few days before mouth opening and the onset of active prey capture. Despite their minute size, these larvae display a well-developed notochord and functional eye pigmentation at birth, facilitating immediate entry into the planktonic community.

Longevity in Sebastes entomelas is considerable, with the maximum lifespan estimated at 60 years [am = 60 years] under the cool water temperatures (5.6 °C [T = 5.6 °C]) characteristic of their preferred depth range. This exceptional lifespan is consistent with the broader life-history pattern observed in the genus Sebastes, where many species exhibit slow senescence and extended reproductive windows. Otolith-based age determination from archival specimens collected in Alaskan waters has confirmed individuals exceeding five decades of age, placing this species among the longer-lived teleosts in the North Pacific. The combination of late maturity, high annual fecundity, and extreme longevity defines a bet-hedging life-history strategy that buffers the population against years of poor recruitment. The oldest documented individuals continue to reproduce actively, indicating that reproductive senescence is either absent or minimal until the very final years of life. This remarkable longevity underscores the importance of conservative harvest management for this species, as recovery from overfishing can require multiple decades.
